quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten quick checks on the vocabulary of an export yarn costing: variable cost, contribution, fixed frame cost and break-even.

questions.q: In this costing, which test decides whether a cost is treated as variable?
options: It is paid in US dollars
It is incurred only because the bag is sold
It is paid every month regardless of output
It is charged per container rather than per bag
questions.explain: The lecture's rule is simple: every cost that is incurred because the bag is sold is variable. Currency or the unit of billing does not matter; ocean freight is billed per container in dollars yet it is still variable because no sale means no freight.

questions.q: Which of these is treated as a fixed cost in the yarn export costing?
questions.explain: The frame cost of depreciation, finance and labour is incurred whether or not the bag is sold, so it is fixed per frame per day. Freight, packing and the surcharge all disappear if there is no sale.

questions.q: Contribution per bag is the price per bag minus the total variable cost per bag.
questions.explain: Contribution margin per bag = Rs 5,444.65 − Rs 4,327.89 = Rs 1,116.75 in the lecture. It is what is left to cover fixed cost and profit.

questions.q: What is a standard export yarn bag in this lecture?
questions.explain: Prices per bag are computed for a bag of 100 lb (about 45.4 kg). A student who treats the bag as 100 kg will overstate every per-bag figure by more than double.

questions.q: The break-even price per bag is the price at which…
options: profit per frame per day is zero
the mill ships exactly one container a day
variable cost per bag equals the frame cost
questions.explain: Break-even in this costing is the price where the contribution earned by one frame in a day exactly equals the frame's fixed cost, so profit per frame per day is zero. Zero contribution per bag would mean a much larger loss.

questions.q: What does the export development surcharge depend on?
options: The number of bags per container
The sale value of the yarn
questions.explain: The surcharge is a small percentage (0.25 %) of the export proceeds, so it rises and falls with the price per bag; it is not linked to freight or raw material.

questions.q: Raw material cost per bag is the cotton price × 100 lb with no further adjustment.
questions.explain: The lecture uses an adjusted cotton cost: the cotton bought must cover the waste removed in spinning, so the cost per lb of yarn is higher than the cost per lb of raw cotton.

questions.q: Why is the frame the unit for comparing contribution with fixed cost?
options: Because frames are sold with the yarn
Because the frame is the scarce productive resource whose daily cost must be recovered
Because each frame makes exactly one bag a day
Because the bank charges are billed per frame
questions.explain: A spinning mill's capacity is its frames; each costs about Rs 14,000 a day whether it runs or not, so the question is whether the bags a frame makes in a day earn at least that much contribution.

questions.q: In the term OPS 10.3 × 0.9 for Ne 20, what does the 0.9 represent?
options: The utilisation or efficiency applied to the frame's rated output
The weight of a bag in kg
questions.explain: OPS (ounces per spindle per shift) gives the rated output; multiplying by 0.9 allows for stoppages and efficiency, giving 9.27 bags per frame per day. The exchange rate and bag weight are separate inputs.

questions.q: Foreign bank charges and ocean freight are first costed per container and then divided by the bags per container.
questions.explain: Both are shown in the per-container column (Rs 15,000 and Rs 30,000) and divided by 400 bags to give Rs 37.50 and Rs 75.00 per bag.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: How price, exchange rate, bags per frame and fixed cost combine, and which way each figure moves.

questions.q: Price per bag in rupees equals…
questions.explain: Convert dollars per kg to rupees per kg, then multiply by the kg in a 100 lb bag (100 ÷ 2.2046 ≈ 45.36 kg). Multiplying by 100 treats the bag as 100 kg.

questions.q: If the exchange rate rises from Rs 60 to Rs 65 per dollar and the dollar price is unchanged, what happens to contribution per bag?
options: It falls because freight in dollars costs more
It rises because the rupee proceeds rise by much more than the dollar-based costs
It is unchanged because both revenue and cost are in dollars
questions.explain: Proceeds per bag are about Rs 5,445 at Rs 60, all of it dollar-based; dollar costs (ocean freight and foreign bank charges) are only about Rs 112 per bag. A weaker rupee therefore raises contribution strongly.

questions.q: Contribution per frame per day is found by…
options: contribution per bag ÷ bags per frame per day
contribution per bag × bags per frame per day
price per bag × bags per frame per day
fixed cost per frame ÷ bags per frame per day
questions.explain: Rs 1,116.75 × 9.27 bags = Rs 10,352 per frame per day. Dividing instead gives a meaningless Rs 120, and using price ignores the variable cost.

questions.q: Profit per frame per day = contribution per frame per day − fixed cost per frame per day.
questions.explain: Rs 10,352 − Rs 14,000 = −Rs 3,648, the loss shown in the lecture. Fixed cost is deducted only once the contribution has been found.

questions.q: If the OPS of the frames rises (more bags per frame per day), what happens to the break-even price per bag?
questions.explain: More bags per frame means the fixed Rs 14,000 is spread over more bags, so less contribution is needed from each bag and the break-even price falls.

questions.q: Which formula gives the contribution per bag needed to break even?
options: Fixed cost per frame per day ÷ bags per frame per day
Fixed cost per frame per day × bags per frame per day
Total variable cost per bag ÷ bags per frame per day
Price per bag − fixed cost per frame per day
questions.explain: The frame must earn Rs 14,000 a day from 9.27 bags, so each bag must contribute 14,000 ÷ 9.27 ≈ Rs 1,510. Add the variable cost (with the surcharge adjusted) to get the break-even price.

questions.q: The total daily profit or loss of the mill is found by…
options: profit per frame per day × total frames
profit per frame per day ÷ total frames
questions.explain: −Rs 3,648 per frame × 46 frames = −Rs 167,794 per day in the lecture. Every frame is assumed to run the same count at the same price.

questions.q: A per-container charge of Rs X becomes a per-bag charge of…
questions.explain: A container carries 400 bags, so each bag bears one four-hundredth of a container-level charge. Dividing by 100 or 45.36 confuses bags with pounds or kilograms.

questions.q: Because the export development surcharge is a percentage of the price, raising the price by Rs 100 raises contribution per bag by exactly Rs 100.
questions.explain: The surcharge of 0.25 % also rises, by Rs 0.25, so contribution rises by Rs 99.75. Small, but it is why the break-even price is slightly higher than variable cost plus required contribution.

questions.q: Converting a break-even price per bag back to US$ per kg requires dividing by…
options: the exchange rate and the kg per bag
the bags per container and the exchange rate
questions.explain: Rs 5,839 per bag ÷ 45.36 kg ÷ Rs 60 per US$ = US$ 2.145 per kg. Dividing by the exchange rate alone gives dollars per bag, not per kg.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Work through the lecture's numbers and some new ones: price per bag, per-bag export charges, contribution and break-even.

questions.q: Ne 20 yarn sells at US$ 2.00 per kg and the exchange rate is Rs 60 per dollar. What is the price in Rs per kg?
questions.explain: US$ 2.00 × Rs 60 = Rs 120 per kg, the basis figure in the lecture.

questions.q: At Rs 120 per kg, what is the price of one bag of 100 lb? Take 1 kg = 2.2046 lb and answer to the nearest rupee.
questions.explain: 100 lb ÷ 2.2046 = 45.36 kg; 45.36 × Rs 120 = Rs 5,443 (the lecture shows Rs 5,444.65 using a slightly different conversion factor).

questions.q: Ocean freight for a container is US$ 500 at Rs 60 per dollar and the container carries 400 bags. What is the ocean freight per bag?
questions.explain: US$ 500 × 60 = Rs 30,000 per container; ÷ 400 bags = Rs 75.00 per bag.

questions.q: The export development surcharge is 0.25 % of the price. On a bag priced at Rs 5,444.65, what is the surcharge (to the nearest paisa)?
Price per bag is Rs 5,444.65 and total variable cost per bag is Rs 4,327.89. What is the contribution per bag?
questions.explain: Contribution = price − variable cost = Rs 5,444.65 − Rs 4,327.89 = Rs 1,116.76 (shown as 1,116.75 in the sheet).

questions.q: A Ne 20 frame produces 10.3 bags per day at rated output and runs at 90 % efficiency. How many bags does it make per day?
questions.explain: 10.3 × 0.9 = 9.27 bags per frame per day.

questions.q: Contribution per bag is Rs 1,116.75 and a frame makes 9.27 bags a day. The frame's fixed cost is Rs 14,000 a day. What is the profit or loss per frame per day (loss as a negative number, to the nearest rupee)?
questions.explain: Contribution per frame = 1,116.75 × 9.27 = Rs 10,352; minus Rs 14,000 fixed cost = −Rs 3,648, a loss.

questions.q: If each of 46 frames loses Rs 3,648 a day, what is the mill's total daily loss (enter as a positive number of rupees)?
questions.explain: Rs 3,648 × 46 = Rs 167,808 (the lecture shows Rs 167,794 because it carries unrounded figures).

questions.q: The frame needs Rs 14,000 contribution a day from 9.27 bags. Ignoring the surcharge, what contribution per bag is required?
questions.explain: 14,000 ÷ 9.27 = Rs 1,510 per bag. Rs 1,117 is the current contribution, which is why the frame loses money.

questions.q: The break-even price is Rs 5,839 per bag of 100 lb. Taking 1 kg = 2.2046 lb and Rs 60 per dollar, what is this in US$ per kg (to three decimals)?
questions.explain: Rs 5,839 ÷ 45.36 kg = Rs 128.7 per kg; ÷ 60 = US$ 2.145 per kg, as in the lecture.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Decisions a spinning mill's marketing office faces every day: which price to accept, which cost to cut, when a frame should keep running.

questions.q: A buyer offers US$ 2.10 per kg for Ne 20 when the break-even is US$ 2.145. The mill's frames are otherwise idle. What is the best advice?
options: Refuse: any price below break-even must be refused
Accept: the price covers all variable costs and contributes towards the fixed frame cost that is incurred anyway
Accept only if the buyer pays the freight
questions.explain: The frame's Rs 14,000 fixed cost is incurred whether it runs or not. US$ 2.10 gives a positive contribution per bag, so running reduces the loss. Idle frames still carry depreciation, finance and labour.

questions.q: Which single change would improve profit per frame most, in the lecture's own words?
options: Raising the price, the exchange rate or the OPS
Shipping 380 bags instead of 400 per container
questions.explain: Postage (Rs 2.50) and local bank charges (Rs 4.50) are trivial per bag. Price, exchange rate and OPS move the proceeds and the bags per frame, which is where the money is.

questions.q: The forwarder quotes a container that holds only 300 bags instead of 400. What happens to the ocean freight per bag?
questions.explain: Rs 30,000 ÷ 300 = Rs 100 per bag instead of Rs 75. Container charges are fixed per box, so fewer bags in a box means more per bag.

questions.q: If cotton prices rise, the raw material per bag rises and the break-even price in US$ rises too.
questions.explain: Raw material is Rs 4,057 of the Rs 4,328 variable cost per bag; a higher cotton cost raises variable cost rupee for rupee, and so the price needed to break even.

questions.q: The rupee weakens from Rs 60 to Rs 63 per dollar overnight. A marketing manager says the mill's costing must be redone. Which items change in rupees?
options: Only ocean freight and foreign bank charges
Price per bag, ocean freight, foreign bank charges and the surcharge on the price
Nothing, because the contract is in dollars
questions.explain: Every dollar-denominated line converts at the new rate: proceeds, ocean freight and foreign bank charges. The surcharge follows the rupee proceeds. Local freight, packing and cotton are unchanged.

questions.q: A mill has 46 frames and a daily loss of about Rs 168,000 at US$ 2.00. A buyer will pay US$ 2.20 for the whole output. Roughly what happens?
options: The mill moves to a profit of roughly Rs 60,000 a day
The loss is unchanged because freight rises
The mill makes about Rs 500,000 a day
questions.explain: Break-even is US$ 2.145, so US$ 2.20 is 5.5 cents above it: 0.055 × 60 × 45.36 ≈ Rs 150 more per bag, × 9.27 bags × 46 frames ≈ Rs 64,000 a day profit after allowing for the surcharge.

questions.q: A costing clerk includes the frame's depreciation in the variable cost per bag. What goes wrong?
options: Contribution per bag is understated and fixed cost is counted twice when the frame cost is deducted again
Nothing, since depreciation is a real cost
The price per bag becomes wrong
questions.explain: Depreciation is already in the Rs 14,000 fixed frame cost. Putting it in the variable cost as well double-counts it and makes a marginally profitable order look loss-making.

questions.q: Two offers: Ne 20 at US$ 2.145 per kg, or Ne 20 at US$ 2.10 with the buyer paying the ocean freight (US$ 500 per container). Which earns more per bag?
options: US$ 2.10 with freight paid, by about Rs 50
questions.explain: The 4.5 cent difference is 0.045 × 60 × 45.36 ≈ Rs 122 less per bag at US$ 2.10, while the freight saved is only Rs 75 per bag (the surcharge difference is a few paisa). Net, the US$ 2.145 offer earns about Rs 47–50 more per bag.

questions.q: Reducing packing cost from Rs 100 to Rs 80 per bag adds Rs 20 to contribution per bag and about Rs 185 per frame per day.
questions.explain: Rs 20 × 9.27 bags per frame per day = Rs 185. Useful, but small against a Rs 3,648 daily loss per frame.

questions.q: The marketing office wants a quick rule for the minimum acceptable dollar price. Which is correct?
options: Variable cost per bag converted to dollars
The price at which contribution per frame per day equals the fixed cost per frame per day
The price that fills a container
questions.explain: That is the break-even price (US$ 2.145 here). Variable cost alone is the floor below which an order should never be taken, but it leaves nothing for the frame cost.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Two-step reasoning across the whole yarn costing: common slips, sensitivity to price and rate, and the logic of break-even.

questions.q: A frame's fixed cost is Rs 14,000 a day and it makes 9.27 bags. Variable cost per bag excluding the surcharge is Rs 4,314.28 and the surcharge is 0.25 % of price. What price per bag breaks even, to the nearest rupee?
A student computes the price per bag as US$ 2 × Rs 60 × 100 = Rs 12,000. What is the error?
options: The exchange rate should be divided, not multiplied
The bag is 100 lb, not 100 kg, so the price should be about Rs 5,445
The price should be per container
questions.explain: 100 lb is only 45.36 kg; 45.36 × Rs 120 = Rs 5,443. Confusing pounds and kilograms more than doubles every per-bag revenue figure.

questions.q: The price rises by one US cent per kg from US$ 2.00 to US$ 2.01 at Rs 60 per dollar. By how much does the price of a 100 lb bag rise? Take 1 kg = 2.2046 lb and answer to the nearest paisa.
questions.explain: 0.01 × 60 = Rs 0.60 per kg; × 45.36 kg per bag = Rs 27.22 per bag. Multiply by 9.27 bags and 46 frames and a single cent is worth about Rs 11,600 a day to the mill.

questions.q: At US$ 2.00 the frame loses Rs 3,648 a day. If the frame is stopped instead, what is the daily result for that frame?
questions.explain: Stopping the frame removes the contribution (Rs 10,352) but not the fixed cost (Rs 14,000). The loss grows from Rs 3,648 to Rs 14,000, which is why loss-making frames keep running in the short run.

questions.q: The exchange rate moves from Rs 60 to Rs 62 per dollar with the price fixed at US$ 2.00 per kg. By roughly how much does the rupee price of a 100 lb bag rise? Use 45.36 kg per bag and answer to the nearest rupee.
questions.explain: Rs 2 extra per dollar × US$ 2 per kg = Rs 4 per kg; × 45.36 kg = Rs 181 per bag. Dollar costs (freight and bank charges, about US$ 1.9 per bag) rise by only about Rs 4.

questions.q: Because 9.27 bags per frame are sold per day, the break-even price per bag is less than the variable cost per bag plus Rs 14,000.
questions.explain: The Rs 14,000 fixed cost is spread over 9.27 bags, so only about Rs 1,510 is added to each bag's variable cost, giving Rs 5,839, not Rs 18,000 or more.

questions.q: Which combination makes the frame profitable with no change in price: (i) OPS up 10 %, (ii) exchange rate up 10 %, (iii) packing cost down 10 %?
questions.explain: A 10 % rise in the rate adds about Rs 540 per bag (proceeds Rs 5,445 less about Rs 112 of dollar costs ≈ Rs 533 net), × 9.27 ≈ Rs 4,900 a day, covering the Rs 3,648 loss. OPS up 10 % adds only 0.927 × 1,117 ≈ Rs 1,035; packing saves Rs 10 a bag.

questions.q: Profit per day for the mill is −Rs 167,794 and profit per frame is −Rs 3,648. What is the reasoning behind the mill figure?
options: Loss per bag × bags per container
Loss per frame × 46 frames, assuming all frames run Ne 20 at this price
questions.explain: −3,648 × 46 ≈ −167,800. The costing assumes the whole mill runs one count at one price; Lecture 17 relaxes this by mixing counts.

questions.q: Local freight is Rs 15,000 per container of 400 bags and local bank charges are Rs 4.50 per bag. What is the combined local freight and local bank charge per bag?
questions.explain: Rs 15,000 ÷ 400 = Rs 37.50 local freight per bag; plus Rs 4.50 = Rs 42.00 per bag.

questions.q: A trainee argues that since the mill loses money at US$ 2.00, variable cost per bag must exceed the price. Where is the flaw?
options: Price exceeds variable cost by Rs 1,117; the loss arises because that contribution, times 9.27 bags, is below the Rs 14,000 fixed frame cost
The loss is caused by the surcharge
questions.explain: A positive contribution and a loss can coexist whenever contribution per frame per day is below fixed cost per frame per day. The contribution is real; it is simply not large enough.
